title: Work Market 2026: AI, WorkMarket & Key Hiring Trends
summary: Get the November 2026 work market picture: WorkMarket by ADP reviews, AI hiring data, and tips for adapting your workforce strategy.
body_markdown:
The world of work has changed. Today’s talent pool isn’t just about full time employees, it’s a varied blend of W 2 staff, 1099 contractors, and freelancers from around the globe. This blended model, often called the extended workforce, offers incredible flexibility but also creates new management challenges. To manage this new reality, businesses rely on a specialized type of software, and for years, a key player in this work market has been WorkMarket.


This guide looks at WorkMarket as a foundational platform and then zooms out to the broader U.S. job market, offering a clear picture of the trends shaping how companies hire and grow today.


**TLDR:**


- WorkMarket (now WorkMarket by ADP) is a Freelance Management System that handles contractor onboarding, payments, and tax compliance in one place.
- Business users rate WorkMarket 4.2/5 on G2, but contractors rate it 1.9/5 on Trustpilot, citing slow payments and extra fees.
- The U.S. job market is slowing, not collapsing. There were 7.2 million openings in August 2025, with wage growth at 4% year over year.
- In 2025, 59% of roles impacted by AI were augmented instead of eliminated, making human judgment and AI literacy your most valuable skills.
- Bolto combines AI-powered recruiting, EOR, and payroll into one system for startups that need to hire and scale quickly without multiple vendors.


## What is WorkMarket? A Look at the Software


WorkMarket, now known as WorkMarket by ADP, is a cloud based workforce management platform. It was built to give companies a single system for managing both their traditional employees and their independent contractors. Think of it as a unified dashboard for the entire talent ecosystem.


Organizations use the WorkMarket platform to handle the complete lifecycle of their freelance talent, including:


- Onboarding and verification
- Assigning projects and tasks
- Tracking work in real time
- Processing payments and keeping tax compliance on track


At its core, WorkMarket is a[Freelance Management System (FMS)](https://www.bolto.com/resources/intro-to-freelance-recruiting) , HR technology that automates contractor paperwork so companies can scale a flexible workforce. Its mobile app, available on iOS and Android, lets independent contractors manage work on the go. Contractors receive work assignment notifications, can apply, decline, or counteroffer, and can self-onboard by adding payment and tax information. On site, they check in and out of job sites and upload deliverables like photos and documents, then submit invoices and request payments or reimbursements without leaving the app.


## The History of WorkMarket


WorkMarket was founded in May 2010 in New York City by Jeffrey Leventhal, just as the gig economy gained momentum. Backed by venture firms like Union Square Ventures and Spark Capital, the company raised over $50 million. It had around 156 employees prior to its broader integration into ADP.


The turning point came in January 2018, when HR and payroll giant ADP acquired WorkMarket for an undisclosed sum. The deal gave ADP’s clients a native solution for managing a growing contingent workforce.


## Recognition and Industry Standing


Upon acquiring the company, ADP praised WorkMarket as a “leading cloud based workforce management solution provider” and a “proven expert in freelancer management.” This endorsement solidified its reputation as a pioneer in the space.


The platform’s credibility is also reflected in its diverse client base, which includes everything from small businesses to global Fortune 500 enterprises. On the software review site G2, WorkMarket holds a 4.2 out of 5 star rating from business users who praise its utility for managing on demand talent. With the acquisition, ADP became the only major Human Capital Management (HCM) provider at the time to offer a single, integrated system for managing both employees and contingent workers.


## WorkMarket by ADP Reviews: A Tale of Two Users


User reviews for the WorkMarket platform paint a divided picture, largely split between the companies who use it and the individual freelancers who get paid through it.


On business focused review sites like G2, administrators and managers generally rate it well (4.2/5 stars) and appreciate the centralized system for assigning work and processing payments. On consumer sites like Trustpilot, the average rating drops to 1.9 out of 5. Common complaint themes include slow customer support, payments taking weeks to arrive, accounts restricted or closed with little explanation, and extra fees charged to contractors. Many freelancers feel the tool is built for the client company, not the end worker, a familiar tension in the work market between business needs and the independent contractor experience.

## The U.S. Job Market is Slowing, Not Collapsing


Understanding any tool for the work market requires understanding the work market itself. Recently, you’ve likely heard a lot of conflicting news. The consensus among economists is that the U.S. job market is **slowing, not collapsing** .


While job growth has cooled sharply from its red hot pace, we are not seeing the massive, widespread job losses that define a recession. For example, the economy is still adding jobs each month, just at a much slower rate. The unemployment rate has ticked up but remains low by historical standards. A slowdown feels unsettling, but it’s a deceleration, not a free fall.


## The Big Picture: Why is Hiring Cooling Off?


Zooming out, the slowdown isn’t happening in a vacuum. Several major forces are at play.


First, **structural changes** like an aging population and slower immigration mean the labor force itself isn’t growing as fast. The economy now needs fewer jobs each month just to keep unemployment stable. Second, a massive wave of **investment in AI and automation** is boosting productivity. Companies can now achieve growth with fewer new hires. We’re seeing a rare combination of strong GDP growth with weaker job creation. Finally, many large corporations that over hired during the pandemic are now rightsizing their workforce.


## The Great Recalibration: AI’s Role in the New Work Market


The rise of Artificial Intelligence is more than another trend. It is a fundamental shift reshaping industries and jobs at every level. While the World Economic Forum estimated that AI would replace 85 million jobs by 2025, it is also expected to create 97 million new roles by the end of 2025. This transformation is creating a new set of rules for the work market.


### AI Tool Adoption Across Industries


AI is no longer a pilot project, it is a core business tool. Adoption varies by sector. In a controlled GitHub experiment, developers using an AI coding assistant finished a coding task 55% faster than developers working without one.


### The Impact on Entry Level Jobs


Generative AI is having a major and disproportionate impact on early career workers. A Stanford study found that U.S. employment for early career professionals in AI exposed fields has fallen, as AI can now execute 50 to 60 percent of typical junior tasks like report drafting and data cleaning. This doesn’t mean entry level jobs are disappearing, but that they are being redesigned. Companies are shifting junior employees away from automatable tasks and toward higher value activities like client advisory work, fraud investigation, and problem framing.


### Job Security in the Age of AI


The narrative around AI is shifting from job replacement to job transformation. While a 2023 Goldman Sachs Research report on generative AI and economic growth estimated that AI could expose the equivalent of 300 million full-time jobs to automation, it also pointed to the potential for new jobs and a productivity boom. The key is that while specific tasks are being automated, very few jobs can be *fully* automated. This creates a demand for workers who can collaborate with AI, using their human judgment to interpret what the machine produces. In 2025, 59% of roles impacted by AI in the United States were augmented instead of eliminated.


### Career Readiness and Key Skills for an AI Driven Workforce


The rapid evolution of the workplace means that career readiness now depends on a new set of skills. The World Economic Forum’s Future of Jobs Report 2023 estimated that 44 percent of workers’ core skills would be disrupted within five years. To stay relevant, professionals must develop both technical and human centric abilities.


**1. AI Literacy:** This is the foundational skill. It’s the ability to understand what AI is, how it works, and how to use it effectively and ethically. AI literate employees can identify opportunities for automation, critically review AI outputs, and use the technology to innovate instead of simply following instructions. This literacy is becoming as important as digital literacy was a generation ago.


**2. Critical Thinking and Ethical Judgment:** As AI generates answers instantly, the ability to question those answers becomes invaluable. Professionals need to analyze AI outputs for bias, validate information, and make well rounded decisions that an algorithm can’t. This includes understanding the ethical implications of AI, from data privacy to algorithmic bias.


**3. “Human” Skills:** AI excels at data processing, but it cannot replicate human creativity, emotional intelligence, or complex communication. These skills are becoming a key differentiator. Empathy, adaptability, and collaboration matter most for managing teams, building client relationships, and handling the changes AI brings.


**4. A Mindset of Continuous Learning:** Estimates of how quickly skills lose value vary by source and field, with some industry research putting the half life of a technical skill at roughly two and a half to five years. Whatever the exact number, the most important capability is the willingness to constantly learn and adapt. This involves adopting a growth mindset and actively seeking opportunities to upskill.


## The Job Market By the Numbers


To ground the discussion in facts, let’s look at the key statistics from BLS JOLTS data and other sources that define the current work market.


- **Job Growth:** Monthly job gains have fallen from hundreds of thousands in 2022 to just tens of thousands in late 2025.
- **Unemployment Rate:** The rate has climbed from a 50 year low but remains well below recessionary peaks (like 10% in 2009).
- **Job Openings:** There were about 7.2 million job openings in August 2025. For every unemployed person, there is roughly one available job, a sign of a more balanced market.
- **Quits Rate:** The rate at which workers voluntarily leave their jobs has fallen, suggesting workers are more cautious about job hopping.
- **Wage Growth:** Pay increases have moderated to around 4% year over year, down from 5 to 6% previously.


## The “Yes, But” Reality of Today’s Labor Market


The current situation is full of contradictions, best described with a series of “yes, but” statements.


- **Yes** , unemployment is still low, **but** public anxiety about the job market is at its highest level since the 2008 recession.
- **Yes** , the economy is growing, **but** that growth isn’t creating many new jobs due to productivity gains from automation and AI.
- **Yes** , some sectors like government and healthcare are hiring, **but** others like manufacturing and tech are shedding jobs.
- **Yes** , AI is automating many tasks, **but** it is also creating new roles focused on AI management, ethics, and strategy.


This mixed reality means there is no single, simple story. The health of the work market depends heavily on your industry and location.


## A Reality Check on Job Market Fears


With so much uncertainty, it’s easy for fear to outpace facts. A reality check is in order. The current slowdown is a cooling off from an unsustainably hot period, not a repeat of 2008 or 2020. Layoffs are concentrated in specific sectors, not spread across the entire economy. Most importantly, consumer spending has remained resilient, suggesting that while people are worried, their financial situations have not collapsed. The data points to an adjustment period, not a catastrophe.


## The Bottom Line for Today’s Evolving Work Market


So, what is the key takeaway? **The U.S. job market is recalibrating to a new normal driven by economic changes and AI.** This new era demands more strategy from both employers and workers.


For businesses, especially startups, agility is everything. The slowdown is a signal to operate more efficiently. Instead of racing to hire full time staff, many are turning to flexible talent models, building teams with a core of employees and a ring of expert contractors. WorkMarket was founded in 2010 in New York City. It was acquired by ADP in 2018 and now operates as “WorkMarket, an ADP Company.” To get in touch, your best bet is to go through the official WorkMarket or ADP websites, as they handle all sales and support inquiries.

No, based on current data, the U.S. job market is not in a recession. While hiring has slowed down and unemployment has risen slightly, the economy is still creating jobs, and the unemployment rate remains low by historical standards. It is more accurately described as a slowdown or a cooling off period.
